html:
The Inuit are the Indigenous people of the Arctic from northern Alaska across Canada to Greenland. They speak Inuit languages of the Eskimo-Aleut family, close kin of the Yup'ik of Alaska and Siberia.

They descend from the Thule people, who spread east from Alaska after about 1000 in the Thule migration and replaced the older Paleo-Inuit or Dorset culture. They brought dog sleds, skin boats, the kayak and the harpoon for whales and seals. In Greenland they met the Norse settlers, whose colony died out in the 1400s while the Inuit stayed.

Life in 1492 turned on the seasons:

  • winter on the sea ice, hunting seals at breathing holes and living in snow houses or sod houses;
  • summer on land, fishing char and hunting caribou;
  • whale hunts in open water where the ice allowed.

Contact with whalers, missionaries and the fur trade grew from the 1700s. In the 1900s Canada moved many Inuit into settlements. Self-rule followed: Greenland home rule in 1979 and the territory of Nunavut in Canada in 1999.
